questions_and_answers.question: What is often more difficult than opening a conversation?
In daily encounters with Japanese neighbors, what may sometimes happen with greetings?

answers.answer: They may become longer than you really want them to be

questions_and_answers.question: Unless the other person shows a sign of wanting to go, what might the friendly Japanese feel?

answers.answer: That s/he has to continue the conversation
That s/he must switch to English
Well, excuse me (I have to go).

questions_and_answers.question: Why would 'Sayoonara' sound a little odd when closing such an encounter?

answers.answer: It is usually used when the speaker thinks s/he will not meet the hearer again, at least on the same day
It is only used in the morning

questions_and_answers.question: If a similar conversation takes place late in the evening, what is also appropriate in place of 'mata'?
What expressions does someone in a rush need to close a long conversation?

answers.answer: 'Excuse me, I have to go now,' or 'Well, I'll see you,' or the like

questions_and_answers.question: Can you use 'Gomen kudasai' to close an encounter late in the evening?

answers.answer: Yes, you can use Gomen kudasai there, too

questions_and_answers.question: In the sample dialog, how does Jonson close the encounter after the weather comment?

articles.text:
3. How to close an encounter

Often it is more difficult to close a conversation than to open one. This is especially true when speaking a foreign language. In your daily encounters with your Japanese neighbors, it may sometimes happen that greetings become longer than you really want them to be. Look at the following:

Nihonjin: Jonson-san, ohayoo gozaimasu.
Jonson: Ohayoo gozaimasu.
Nihonjin: Ima odekake desu ka?
Jonson: Ee.
Nihonjin: Kyoo wa ii otenki desu ne.
Jonson: Soo desu ne. Ja, mata.

Unless Jonson-san shows some sign that he wants to go, the friendly Japanese may feel that s/he has to continue the conversation, although to Jonson-san the conversation may have already become too long (he may be in a rush to get to his office). The expressions Jonson-san needs are 'Excuse me, I have to go now,' or 'Well, I'll see you,' or the like. The following are expressions that can be used in the above situation:

Jaa, mata.            Well, (see you) again.
Jaa, gomen kudasai.   Well, excuse me (I have to go).

Note that Sayoonara would sound a little odd in the above situation, for it is usually used when the speaker thinks s/he will not meet the hearer again, at least on the same day.

If a similar conversation takes place late in the evening, Oyasuminasai 'Good night' is also appropriate in place of mata 'again.' You can use Gomen kudasai here, too.
